\section[\texorpdfstring{\sk{वर्तते} (vartate)}{वर्तते (vartate)}]{\sk{वर्तते} (vartate) — is present, exists}

\label{lesson:SA-C232-vartate}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Sanskrit for a guest house, then the Sanskrit for a stay abroad, a journey.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{वर्तते}}
\textbf{\sk{वर्तते}} — \emph{vartate} — \textquotedblleft{}is present, exists\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{vartate} is the present of the root √vṛt, \textquotedblleft{}to turn, roll\textquotedblright{}, and then \textquotedblleft{}to proceed, take place, exist\textquotedblright{} (MW). MW compares Latin \emph{vertere}, \textquotedblleft{}to turn\textquotedblright{}, and German \emph{werden}, \textquotedblleft{}to become\textquotedblright{}. It is the verb inside \emph{parivartayati}, \textquotedblleft{}changes\textquotedblright{}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for this chapter.
\end{grammarlens}

\raggedright

  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{vartate}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} say \emph{vartate}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Sanskrit for a guest house, then the Sanskrit for a stay abroad, a journey, then say \emph{vartate} again
\end{itemize}

\section[\texorpdfstring{\sk{जायते} (jāyate)}{जायते (jāyate)}]{\sk{जायते} (jāyate) — is born, arises}

\label{lesson:SA-C232-jayate}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Sanskrit for a stay abroad, a journey, then the Sanskrit for is present.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{जायते}}
\textbf{\sk{जायते}} — \emph{jāyate} — \textquotedblleft{}is born, arises\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{jāyate} is the present of the root √jan, \textquotedblleft{}to be born\textquotedblright{} (MW), the root of \emph{jantu}, \textquotedblleft{}creature\textquotedblright{}. MW compares Latin \emph{gignere}, \textquotedblleft{}to beget\textquotedblright{}. It lives on as Gujarati \emph{jāvũ}, \textquotedblleft{}to be born\textquotedblright{} (CDIAL 5204).
\end{cousinweb}

\section[\texorpdfstring{\sk{म्रियते} (mriyate)}{म्रियते (mriyate)}]{\sk{म्रियते} (mriyate) — dies}

\label{lesson:SA-C232-mriyate}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Sanskrit for is present, then the Sanskrit for is born.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{म्रियते}}
\textbf{\sk{म्रियते}} — \emph{mriyate} — \textquotedblleft{}dies\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{mriyate} is the present of the root √mṛ, \textquotedblleft{}to die\textquotedblright{} (MW; CDIAL 10383). The root is inherited from Indo-European: MW compares Latin \emph{morior}, \textquotedblleft{}I die\textquotedblright{}, and \emph{mors}, \textquotedblleft{}death\textquotedblright{}. Hindi \emph{marnā} probably continues the sister form \emph{marate}, CDIAL 9871 says.
\end{cousinweb}

\section[\texorpdfstring{\sk{नश्यति} (naśyati)}{नश्यति (naśyati)}]{\sk{नश्यति} (naśyati) — is lost, perishes}

\label{lesson:SA-C232-nasyati}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Sanskrit for is born, then the Sanskrit for dies.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{नश्यति}}
\textbf{\sk{नश्यति}} — \emph{naśyati} — \textquotedblleft{}is lost, perishes\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{naśyati} is the present of the root √naś, \textquotedblleft{}to be lost, perish, vanish\textquotedblright{} (MW). MW compares Latin \emph{nex}, \textquotedblleft{}violent death\textquotedblright{}, and \emph{nocēre}, \textquotedblleft{}to harm\textquotedblright{}. It lives on as Hindi \emph{nasnā}, \textquotedblleft{}to be lost, flee\textquotedblright{} (CDIAL 7027).
\end{cousinweb}

\section[\texorpdfstring{\sk{कुप्यति} (kupyati)}{कुप्यति (kupyati)}]{\sk{कुप्यति} (kupyati) — gets angry}

\label{lesson:SA-C232-kupyati}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Sanskrit for dies, then the Sanskrit for is lost.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{कुप्यति}}
\textbf{\sk{कुप्यति}} — \emph{kupyati} — \textquotedblleft{}gets angry\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{kupyati} is the present of the root √kup, \textquotedblleft{}to be moved, swell with rage\textquotedblright{} (MW). It first meant \textquotedblleft{}is agitated\textquotedblright{} and then \textquotedblleft{}is angry\textquotedblright{} (CDIAL 3299). Hindi \emph{kupnā} means \textquotedblleft{}to become angry\textquotedblright{}.
\end{cousinweb}
